title: Far From Heaven
full_review:
The seemingly ideal life of an affluent housewife in 1957 Connecticut is shattered when she discovers her husband is attracted to other men in the sensitive melodrama "Far From Heaven" (Focus).

Writer-director Todd Haynes pays homage to the films of Douglas Sirk, especially "All That Heaven Allows" and "Imitation of Life," by crafting an exquisite melodrama of the kind Sirk did best -- but bringing out themes that were not as openly addressed in the movies of a half-century ago.

One might expect that Haynes would use a campy tone or turn the film into parody, but he does not. He respects his characters as they come up against societal barriers, and in focusing on their humanity has crafted a wistful, even poignant tale that lingers in the memory.

The movie opens on a crisply glorious autumn day with Cathy Whitaker (Julianne Moore), the serenely gracious wife of successful executive Frank (Dennis Quaid), with her two young children at their beautiful Hartford home tended by a black maid (Viola Davis). Frank works long hours and when the police call her to pick him up after a fender-bender she isn't judgmental that he had been drinking.

The next day, while being interviewed in her home for a photo society spread she is startled to see a black man on her property. She confronts Raymond (Dennis Haysbert) and apologizes when she learns that he is the new gardener. When she later sees widower Raymond at a modern art exposition she discusses the paintings with him, oblivious of her friends' highly disapproving stares.

One evening when, as usual, Frank is delayed, she surprises him at his office with a hot dinner only to be shocked at finding him kissing another man. Horrified, he insists on going for therapy to end his homosexual urges and she keeps it secret, remaining supportive even as his increased drinking and emotional distance terrify her.

Raymond, sensing her misery, tries to cheer her with a ride to pick up garden supplies and lunch in his part of town but that backfires enormously when a gossipy neighbor sees them and tells everyone. Scorned by all, a panicked Cathy promises her furious husband she will never speak to Raymond again. But further consequences are to follow, and Frank and Cathy's romantic holiday escape to Miami takes unexpected turns.

Haynes delivers an insightful look at the tensions simmering below the facade of what would appear to be the ideal nuclear family. He treats his characters sympathetically: the husband struggling with his sexual orientation, the wife fearful of losing her husband and of her attraction to Raymond, who believes people can see beyond skin color -- until harsh reality deals him a glancing blow.

Haysbert's performance as the gardener is quietly powerful but Moore carries the picture with her soft voice, earnest expressions and genteel movements perfectly conveying her character's sincerity and fragility. Cathy's essential sweetness shines through in a delicate, skilled portrayal. Nor do Moore or Haysbert need much dialogue to get across their doomed romantic yearning: a soulful glance, a feathery touch of hands says it all.

Troubling as the subject is, the homosexual content is handled with extreme restraint. And not to be overlooked is the careful matching of technique to aesthetics. Some may say Haynes directed each frame to within an inch of its life but there is no denying that the autumn-hued, sun-dappled cinematography is quite beautiful, the production design meticulous and the period costumes remarkable. The mere rustle of Cathy's hoop skirts as she walks suggests the hushed community in which she lives where homophobia and racism simply are not acceptable topics.

The filmmaker however allows us to look at that 1950s society not with condescension based on our more "sophisticated" contemporary perspective, but in a thoughtful way that prompts us to consider and hopefully reject our own prejudices.

Because of a brief homosexual kiss and implied affair, fleeting violence, alcohol abuse, some profanity and an instance of rough language, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
(
2002
)
